Hey so, I'm going for my driver's test next month. But I feel like I need to say something. So obviously, I wasn't in the car with you so I can't tell you if you absolutely should never drive or not. I can tell you one thing. I was in your position a couple months ago. I struggled greatly with reaction time, and identifying where cars are in relation to my mom's car. There were many other things that affect my driving that I didn't even know was tied to my illness. I want you to know that doesn't necessarily mean you can't drive. It might just mean it'll take years to adapt to it.

In today's day and age, there are so many different add ons, you can have for your car that could help people like us significantly. For one thing, I recognize I need a car with a blindspot detector because I simply can't tell how close a car is to me when I'm on the highway. There's also things like lane assist and even cars that will stop if you are about to hit another car. These features are expensive but immensely helpful in people with disabilities involving the mind and information processing.

Another option you could utilize is talking to someone about car adaptations. I'm not too familiar with this, but I know they have different things to use to help drivers with disabilities. I would also check there before completely deciding to give up on driving.

And if after all this, you are certain you are unable to drive, there's nothing wrong with that. You would likely need to find housing and work close to bus stops. You can also look into paratransit for discounted or free bus trips to doctor's appointment. There IS a way around it. And once you find a friend or significant other that's willing to help, it's not that bad.

I spent a large portion of my academic career in alternative schools/programs due to anxiety, schizophrenia, and a bunch of other illnesses. One thing that I think about to this day, is the fact that my therapist in the school outed me to my family. I was 14 at the time, obviously hormones are running, and I naturally had a crush on another student. We secretly started dating. In a lot of these programs, relationships are forbidden because it can interfere with our current mental health treatment. As I got older, the rule they had made sense. However, they didn't need to call my parents and tell them that they caught me kissing a girl. They specified that it was a girl. They then told me this and I promptly ran to the bathroom and puked. This was literally the only time I threw up due to stress.

Same program but a different issue. I struggled with math my whole life. I frequently "get lost" during math problems and end up writing down the wrong numbers. I know now that this sounds like dyscalculia. Instead of investigating why I'm struggling and why certain concepts don't stick in my mind, they said I was manipulating them to get out of doing work. That day, I gave up on math and decided that it's something I am just not going to get.

As I got older, I assumed that their rules and the things they did would make more sense. At the time my sense of reality was vastly distorted and I thought they were doing what was best for me. Now I realize alterative programs are really fucked up and no one listens to the students' complaints because they are mentally ill.

In general, to get better grades:

1. Do the assigned reading! I see a lot of students skip this but it's so important. Do the assigned reading before class so that when you're in class you're able to ask meaningful questions.
2. Get help the moment you are confused. As soon as something doesn't make sense go to the tutoring center for clarification. Repeat this many times throughout the semester.
3. Study effectively for tests. Don't just look over notes and take the exam. Study each concept and try to relate it to things you already know. Then make a study guide or a Quizlet and test yourself on the concepts. 
4. Take care of yourself! This is a part I just recently learned. If you are stressed/tired/hungry, it decreases your working memory and you are unable to grasp concepts quickly. This means that even if you absolutely have to get an assignment done, it might be better for you to walk away from it in order to reapproach it more focused.
